Hast.et: 16th century, from Middle Low German hāst, from Middle Dutch haest, a borrowing from Old French haste, itself borrowed from Frankish *hai(f)st, from Proto-Germanic *haifstiz. See English haste for more.

Hase.et: From Middle High German has(e), from Old High German haso, from Proto-West Germanic *hasō, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from an Indo-European root originally meaning grey.
German and Jewish surname, from the noun meaning "hare" (see Etymology 1 above). Occasionally calqued from Lower Sorbian Zajac, of the same meaning.
From the same root as the animal name, meaning “grey”, an adjective Proto-West Germanic *hasu (“grey”).

Hasenscharte.et: From Middle High German hasinscharte. By surface analysis, Hase (“hare”) + -n- + Scharte (“notch”). So called because of the similarity to the outer form of a hare’s lip. Compare already Old English hærsceard.

Hass.et: From Middle High German haȥ, from Old High German haȥ. Compare Dutch haat, English hate, Danish had; also Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐍄𐌹𐍃 (hatis), Old Norse hatr, Old English hete, Old Saxon heti.

Haselnuss.et: From Middle High German haselnuz, from Old High German hasalnuz. Analysable as Hasel + Nuss. Cognate with Dutch hazelnoot, English hazelnut.

Hasel.et: From Middle High German hasel, from Old High German hasal, from Proto-West Germanic *hasl.
Inherited from Middle High German hasel, from Old High German hasala f.

hässlich.et: From Middle High German hezzelich, hazzelich, hazlich, hezlich, from Old High German hazlīh. Equivalent to Hass + -lich.

hastig.et: From Middle High German hastic, hastec. Analysable as Hast + -ig. Compare Middle Low German hastich (whence German Low German hastig, haastig).

Haschee.et: Borrowed from French haschée, a now obsolete spelling of hachée.

Haspel.et: From Middle High German haspel, from Old High German haspil, from Proto-West Germanic *haspilaz, from Proto-Germanic *haspulaz, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *haspijǭ (“clasp; hasp; reel”). More at hasp.
